strengths: Timely and well-motivated contribution: dLLM safety is an emerging area, and the paper provides one of the first systematic analyses of jailbreak vulnerabilities from the perspective of the iterative decoding structure (intra-step remasking bias and inter-step Denoising-path Dependence).

The empirical analysis (Figures 2-5) is insightful and well-designed: the random-remasking control quantifies the Safety-Quality trade-off, and the token injection experiments clearly demonstrate that early-stage tokens decisively shape the final safety outcome.

DiffuGuard is training-free and plug-and-play, with two complementary modules directly grounded in the identified failure modes; the ablation study (Table 2) reasonably supports that the modules address complementary attack types.

Broad evaluation: four dLLMs (LLaDA, Dream, MMaDA, LLaDA-1.5), three harmful datasets, six attack methods, general-capability checks (MMLU/GSM8K/HumanEval), latency analysis, and detailed hyperparameter sensitivity analyses in the appendix.

The paper is clearly written, with a formalized background, full algorithm, judge prompt, and hyperparameter settings that support reproducibility; the ethics statement and limitations section are appropriate.
weaknesses: A key soundness concern in the Block-level Audit: the method requires decomposing the input p0 into a malicious core p_origin and an adversarial template p_template (Algorithm 1 line 'Decompose p0 into p_origin ⊕ p_template'), but the paper never explains how this decomposition is obtained automatically. For real-world jailbreak prompts, the 'original malicious core' is not available, making this assumption potentially unrealistic and central to the claimed defense performance.

Headline numbers are somewhat overstated: the abstract claims a reduction from 47.9% to 14.7%, but 14.7% (17.50% in Table 1) is achieved only when combining DiffuGuard with Self-reminder; DiffuGuard alone yields 27.8%. The paper should present this more transparently.

Baseline defenses are weak and few: only PPL-Filter and Self-reminder are compared. There are no comparisons against other inference-time defenses (e.g., output filtering/refusal-constrained decoding, safety-direction intervention methods such as steering that are natural competitors given the paper's own use of refusal representations).

The Stochastic Annealing Remasking module appears ineffective for its intended target: the ablation shows w/o SAR equals the vanilla ASR on WildJailbreak (23.95 vs 23.95 for LLaDA), contradicting the claim that SAR primarily defends Pre-optimized Prompt Attacks; the defense gains there seem to come from elsewhere.

Evaluation relies solely on GPT-4o-mini as LLM-as-a-Judge without human validation or a second judge, which is risky for safety classification; additionally, sampling at temperature 0.5 introduces variance but no standard deviations or significance tests are reported.

Some experimental design choices weaken conclusions: the GCG suffix is trained on LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct and transfers with ~0% ASR to dLLMs, so that column provides little information; Table 8 shows large non-monotonic effects of γ (e.g., γ=0.95 drastically reducing ASR) that deserve deeper analysis than the one-line explanation.

The repair mechanism (random remasking plus setting logits of previously generated tokens to -inf for all remasked positions) may harm response quality or trigger degenerate outputs (e.g., EOS flooding, as seen in the case study), and the effect on utility is evaluated only at coarse benchmark granularity.

Novelty of the technical components is moderate: stochastic remasking, safety-direction probing via hidden-state divergence (closely following Arditi et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2024b), and logit suppression are all individually known; the contribution is primarily their combination and adaptation to dLLMs.

strengths: Timely and relevant topic: safety of diffusion LLMs is an emerging area with little prior analysis, and the paper's decomposition into intra-step (remasking bias) and inter-step (denoising-path dependence) dynamics offers a plausible and somewhat novel lens on why dLLMs are jailbreakable.

The two exploratory findings are supported by targeted intervention experiments (random remasking sweep in Fig. 3; safe-token injection at different steps in Fig. 5), which motivate the defense design in a principled way rather than being purely heuristic.

Broad empirical coverage: four dLLM families (LLaDA, LLaDA-1.5, Dream, MMaDA), six jailbreak attacks including dLLM-specific ones (PAD, DIJA), plus ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity analyses, and utility/latency checks in the appendix.

The defense is training-free and plug-and-play, with results showing substantial ASR reductions on the dLLM-specific attacks (e.g., PAD/DIJA) and a reasonable ethics statement and limitations section.
weaknesses: Confusing and potentially misleading headline claims: the abstract advertises 47.9% -> 14.7%, but DIFFUGUARD alone only achieves 47.9% -> 27.8% (Section 5.2); on LLaDA-8B, DIFFUGUARD alone (31.13 avg ASR) is actually worse than the simple Self-reminder baseline (30.36). The main results table shows the framework's standalone contribution is modest and inconsistent across models, with the headline number only achievable when combined with Self-reminder.

Weak baseline comparison: only PPL-Filter and Self-reminder are evaluated. Stronger and standard defenses (output filtering, Llama Guard, safety fine-tuning, or even the random remasking control the authors themselves introduced) are missing, making it hard to judge the true added value of the proposed modules.

A key component, Block-level Audit, relies on decomposing the input p0 into p_origin and p_template to compute the Safety Divergence. The paper never explains how this decomposition is obtained automatically for arbitrary user prompts; for attacks without explicit templates (e.g., WildJailbreak, AutoDAN) this seems ill-defined or brittle, and the audit is only applied to the first block, limiting generality.

Sensitivity analyses reveal fragility: the threshold lambda = 0.1 appears very tight, and lambda = 0.3 causes ASR to jump back to 88.46% (LLaDA+PAD), suggesting the defense may not be robust and may be somewhat overfit to the tested attacks.

Evaluation concerns: ASR is judged solely by GPT-4o-mini without human verification or a second judge; some analyses (e.g., Figure 2 logits) use only 5 examples; GCG is trained on LLaMA-3-8B and transferred (and is trivially 0% on the LLaDA family, providing little signal for that column).

Novelty is overstated relative to concurrent/related work: Wen et al. (DIJA) and Zhang et al. (PAD) already demonstrated dLLM jailbreak vulnerabilities; the analysis section, while more mechanistic, builds directly on their observations, and the defense components (randomness injection, confidence-based remasking variants, hidden-state safety divergence) are individually standard techniques.

Results are uneven across models and attacks (e.g., minimal gains on Dream's already-low ASR, weaker performance against AutoDAN), raising questions about when the framework is actually beneficial; the paper's discussion of these inconsistencies is largely post-hoc.

strengths: Timely and well-motivated problem: safety of diffusion LLMs (dLLMs) is an emerging area with few dedicated defenses, and the paper's decomposition of vulnerabilities into intra-step (greedy remasking bias) and inter-step (Denoising-path Dependence) dimensions is a genuinely novel analytical contribution.

The analysis (Sections 3.2-3.3) is empirical and well-designed: the random remasking control experiment quantifies the safety-quality trade-off, and the token injection experiments (Figures 4-5) convincingly demonstrate that early decoding decisions decisively shape final safety.

The proposed DIFFUGUARD modules are directly and logically derived from the analysis findings (annealing schedule tied to early-step importance; audit/repair tied to block-level error propagation), giving the method a principled rather than ad-hoc character.

Comprehensive evaluation: four dLLMs, six attack methods, three harmful-behavior benchmarks, plus ablations (Table 2), hyperparameter sensitivity (Tables 7-8), general-capability checks (MMLU/GSM8K/HumanEval, safe-query false positives), and latency analysis (Figure 7).
Training-free and plug-and-play design is practically valuable; results show strong reductions in ASR against dLLM-specific attacks (PAD, DIJA) with limited degradation of utility.
weaknesses: The Block-level Audit module critically depends on decomposing p0 into p_origin and p_template, but the paper never specifies how this decomposition is performed automatically at inference time (Algorithm 1 simply states 'Decompose p0'). If it relies on knowledge of the attack template or an external decomposition procedure, the method's applicability and threat model need much clearer justification.

Baseline defenses are weak and sparse: only PPL-Filter and Self-reminder are compared. There are no comparisons against stronger or more recent defenses (e.g., Llama Guard, output filtering with safety classifiers, or other dLLM-specific safeguards), making it hard to gauge the method's competitiveness.

Reporting inconsistencies: the abstract claims ASR reduced from 47.9% to 14.7%, while Section 5.2 reports 47.9% to 27.8% for DIFFUGUARD alone; the 14.7% figure appears to correspond to DIFFUGUARD combined with Self-reminder, which conflates the contribution of the proposed method with a simple prompt-level baseline. The Table 1 row labels (+DIFFUGUARD vs +Self-reminder / +DIFFUGUARD) are confusing.

Some attack evaluations are weak: GCG suffixes are trained on LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct and transferred to dLLMs, yielding ASR of 0.00 on three of four models, making that column uninformative. The LLM-as-a-Judge (GPT-4o-mini) is not validated against human annotation.

Analysis experiments rest on very small samples (e.g., Figure 2 uses the first 5 examples), and the safety-quality trade-off is measured only via PPL on jailbreak outputs rather than broader generation-quality metrics.

Repair is applied only to the first generated block, which limits coverage against attacks that contaminate later blocks; the latency claim ('negligible') is evaluated only on two settings while Repair adds 8 extra generation steps.

Individual components have limited novelty in isolation (randomness in decoding, hidden-state-based safety detection are both known); the contribution's strength rests mainly on the dLLM-specific analysis and combination, which some reviewers may view as incremental.

strengths: Timely and well-motivated topic: safety of diffusion LLMs (dLLMs) is an emerging and under-studied area, and the paper's decomposition of vulnerabilities into intra-step (remasking bias) and inter-step (Denoising-path Dependence) dimensions provides a clear, mechanistic analysis framework.

The empirical analysis is well-designed: the random-remasking control experiment (safety-quality trade-off), the 'Sure'/'Sorry' token injection experiments, and the staged intervention (Figure 5) convincingly isolate the claimed mechanisms, and the findings are replicated across four dLLMs in the appendix.

Comprehensive evaluation: four dLLMs, six jailbreak attacks spanning pre-optimized and dLLM-specific (DIJA, PAD) methods, ablation of both modules, hyperparameter sensitivity, general-capability benchmarks (MMLU/GSM8K/HumanEval), latency measurements, and multiple evaluation judges (GPT-4o-mini, LLaMA-Guard, human gold, HarmBench, StrongREJECT), which addresses the common ASR-judge reliability concern.

Notably, the paper includes adaptive attack experiments (multi-sampling, gradient-based optimization of SD, threshold probing) — a step most defense papers omit — showing reasonable robustness and honest residual ASRs rather than cherry-picked numbers.

The defense is training-free, plug-and-play, with quantified minimal impact on utility and inference latency, and the algorithm is fully specified (Appendix E), supporting reproducibility; a code release is promised.
weaknesses: Novelty of the analysis is partially incremental: 'Denoising-path Dependence' closely echoes the known phenomenon that AR LLM safety alignment is shallow and concentrated in early tokens (Qi et al., 2024), and the safety-quality trade-off of added sampling randomness is well established; the paper's appendix acknowledges this, arguing only that parallel decoding makes it more pronounced. The distinction, while reasonable, is argued rather than rigorously demonstrated.

The headline ASR reduction (47.9% -> 14.7%) is achieved only when DiffuGuard is stacked with Self-reminder; standalone DiffuGuard reduces ASR to ~27.8%, which is roughly on par with the simple Self-reminder baseline alone (30.4% average) and, on several settings (e.g., LLaDA + PAD: 59.62 vs. 30.58), standalone DiffuGuard is substantially worse. The abstract/intro presentation overstates the contribution of the proposed method relative to a trivial prompt-level baseline.

The Block-level Audit relies on decomposing the prompt p0 into p_origin ⊕ p_template to compute the safety baseline. It is unclear how this decomposition is obtained in practice for arbitrary jailbreak prompts (which are not always template-decomposable), limiting the generality of the defense beyond in-place-prompting-style attacks; the paper does not specify an automated procedure.

Coverage limitations: the Repair mechanism is only activated for the first generated block, and Table 9 shows adaptive attacks still achieve substantial ASR (44-84% on some models), indicating the defense is not robust to determined white-box attackers; these caveats deserve more prominent discussion than they receive.
Some analysis experiments are very small-scale (e.g., Figure 2 uses the first 5 examples of the dataset), which weakens the evidential weight of the qualitative representation analysis.

GCG transfer results show 0.00 ASR on three of four models even before defense, suggesting some attack configurations do not meaningfully stress the models; the evaluation would benefit from stronger adaptive/optimization-based attacks fully adapted to dLLM tokenization and decoding.

strengths: Timely and relevant topic: safety analysis of diffusion LLMs (dLLMs) is an emerging area, and the intra-step / inter-step decomposition of vulnerabilities is a reasonable organizing framework

The empirical analysis (Section 3) is genuinely informative: the random-remasking control experiment (safety–quality trade-off) and the safe-token injection experiment quantifying 'Denoising-path Dependence' are well-designed and reveal real phenomena of the decoding process

Broad experimental coverage: four dLLMs, six jailbreak methods (including dLLM-specific ones like PAD and DIJA), multiple datasets, an ablation study, hyperparameter sensitivity analyses, and adaptive attack experiments in the appendix
Evaluation robustness checks: the authors validate their LLM-as-a-Judge (GPT-4o-mini) against LLaMA-Guard, human annotation, HarmBench, and StrongREJECT, showing consistent trends
The paper is clearly written, with a clean algorithmic specification (Algorithm 1) and an explicit limitations/ethics discussion
weaknesses: Key methodological assumption is underspecified: the Block-level Audit requires decomposing an arbitrary prompt p0 into a malicious core p_origin and an adversarial template p_template to compute the Safety Divergence. The paper never explains how this decomposition is performed automatically for unseen, arbitrary jailbreak prompts. If it requires knowing the attack template, this is a strong and unrealistic assumption that limits real-world applicability

The defense appears trivially bypassable: the Audit and Repair mechanism is activated ONLY for the first generated block (justified by latency), yet Table 1 shows high vanilla ASR for AutoDAN and other attacks where harmful content is not confined to the first block. A patient attacker can simply place harmful content in later blocks, and the ablation does not test this

Token-level suppression during Guided Regeneration (setting logits of original harmful tokens to -infinity) is a brittle heuristic; paraphrased harmful tokens would evade it, and no analysis of this failure mode is provided

Weak baselines: only PPL-Filter and Self-reminder are compared. Stronger inference-time defenses (output-side safety classifiers, refusal-direction-based methods like Arditi et al., which the authors themselves cite, or model-level defenses) are absent, making it hard to gauge the true contribution

Headline claims overstate the evidence: the abstract claims ASR reduction from 47.9% to 14.7%, but DIFFUGUARD alone achieves 27.8% (Section 5.2); 14.7% requires combining with Self-reminder. The GCG column is essentially vacuous (0.00 baseline ASR for three of four models), yet is included in the table as if it demonstrated defense capability

The defense degrades substantially under the adaptive attacks the authors themselves designed (e.g., LLaDA ASR rises from 24.4% to 44-66%, Dream from 37.3% to 65-85% in Table 9), which partially undermines the 'robust defense' narrative; the adaptive attack suite is also fairly rudimentary

Moderate novelty: injecting randomness into remasking, hidden-state divergence detection, and token suppression are individually simple heuristics; 'Denoising-path Dependence' is closely related to the known finding that AR safety alignment is shallow (Qi et al., 2024), which the authors only discuss in the appendix
Some analyses rest on very small samples: the Figure 2 logit analysis uses only the first 5 examples of the dataset, and human evaluation is limited to 200 samples per dataset

Reproducibility is undermined: the code availability link is empty in both the abstract and the reproducibility statement ('Our code is available at:' with no URL), and the two DIFFUGUARD rows in Table 1 (alone vs. combined with Self-reminder) are labeled confusingly

The Safety Divergence detector's false-positive behavior on unusual but benign prompts is not convincingly analyzed; only a brief mention of safe-query DSR in Figure 6 without breakdown across benign prompt styles

strengths: Timely and significant problem: safety of diffusion LLMs (dLLMs) is an emerging area, and the paper provides one of the first systematic, mechanistic analyses of jailbreak vulnerabilities specific to the dLLM generation paradigm.

The two-dimensional analysis framework (intra-step remasking bias and inter-step Denoising-path Dependence) is well motivated and supported by carefully designed intervention experiments (random remasking control, safe-token injection at varying steps), yielding clear, quantified takeaways (e.g., ASR changes of +76.9%/-24.3%, injection-step decay from 0.2% to 22.8%).

The proposed DIFFUGUARD defense is principled: each module directly addresses a diagnosed failure mode (Stochastic Annealing Remasking for greedy selection bias; Block-level Audit and Repair via Safety Divergence for inter-step error accumulation), rather than being an ad hoc patch.

Comprehensive and unusually thorough evaluation: 4 dLLM families, 6 attack methods spanning pre-optimized and online generative attacks, utility benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K, HumanEval), speed measurements, component ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity, multiple judge models (GPT-4o-mini, LLaMA-Guard, HarmBench, StrongREJECT, human gold), and—importantly—adaptive attacks (multi-sampling, gradient-based SD minimization, threshold probing) that test robustness beyond static benchmarks.

The defense is training-free and plug-and-play with demonstrated negligible latency and utility degradation, making it practically deployable; the ablation cleanly shows the two modules are complementary against different attack paradigms.

Good positioning relative to prior work, including an honest discussion (Appendix F.3) of how the findings relate to known AR LLM phenomena such as shallow safety alignment, and a clear limitations section.
weaknesses: Best headline results depend on combining DIFFUGUARD with Self-reminder: DIFFUGUARD alone reduces average ASR from 47.9% to 27.8%, while the 14.7% figure requires the prompt-level baseline. This confounds the contribution of the proposed mechanism versus simple prompt augmentation, and the abstract/marketing framing could overstate the standalone defense.

Some attack columns are uninformative (GCG ASR is 0.00 for LLaDA/Dream/LLaDA-1.5), so the defense evaluation on those cells cannot demonstrate gains; also the GCG suffix is trained on LLaMA-3-8B and transferred, which is a weak white-box threat model for the defender.

The Block-level Audit relies on decomposing p0 into porigin and ptemplate; how this decomposition is performed automatically and how sensitive SD detection is to decomposition quality (e.g., for subtle or paraphrased attacks) is under-specified in the main text.

The defense introduces multiple hyperparameters (alpha_0, lambda, gamma, extra_steps) tuned per model (e.g., alpha_0=0.7 for Dream vs 0.3 elsewhere), raising questions about generalization to unseen models;Dream's already-low baseline ASR makes part of its evaluation less informative.

No variance reporting: the method is stochastic (random remasking, random block remasking), yet confidence intervals or multiple-seed results are absent, making differences of a few ASR points hard to interpret.

Reproducibility gaps: the code URL in the abstract and the reproducibility statement is left empty; no error bars; some details (threshold calibration for SD across models) are deferred to a config table without derivation.
Minor consistency/clarity issues: the abstract cites 47.9%->14.7% while Section 5.2 reports 47.9%->27.8% (and 27.9% for PAD/DIJA), which can confuse readers; Figure 1 is dense and hard to parse.
